findings.paper_title: Contract Award Agency Procurement Platform - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Agency spend reduced by £7.678m in 2025/26, reaching six-year low of £17.985m
findings.detail: Waltham Forest achieved a major reduction in agency staffing costs from £25.663m in 2024/25 to £17.985m in 2025/26, with agency headcount falling from 415 in June 2024 to 224 by June 2026. The council attributes this to strengthened governance arrangements and focused workforce controls under the Managed Service Provider partnership model initiated in October 2022.
findings.matters: A lender needs evidence that a council can execute cost-reduction programs and maintain financial discipline on major expense categories. This demonstrates Waltham Forest has achieved sustained, material savings through improved governance and strategic workforce management.
findings.figures: £17.985m (2025/26), down from £25.663m (2024/25) and £27.004m (2023/24); agency headcount 224 (June 2026) down from 415 (June 2024); reduction of £7.678m year-on-year
findings.quote: The council closed 2025/26 with agency spend at £17.985m (down from £25.663m in 2024/25), which was the lowest level recorded in six years.

findings.headline: Commercial property and investment income shortfall from 2025/26 of £0.900m still under review, with bad debt risk emerging
findings.detail: The Place directorate reports a breakeven position at month 3 but carries a 'potential pressure within Commercial Property & Investment' pending completion of a 2026/27 rental profile review. The 2025/26 outturn showed a shortfall of £0.900m on commercial income. The review is 'nearly complete' but forecasts are not expected to be refined until month 6.
findings.matters: A £0.900m prior-year commercial income shortfall combined with an incomplete review creates an unquantified downside risk that could materialise mid-year when remediation time is limited.
findings.figures: 2025/26 commercial income shortfall £0.900m; review incomplete until month 6
findings.quote: there is a potential pressure within Commercial Property & Investment - subject to the ongoing full review of the 2026/27 rental profile and potential bad debts. The 2025/26 outturn had a shortfall of £0.900m on commercial income.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account responsive repairs overspend doubled to £2.137m due to Deed of Variation with Morgan Sindall, with further contract risks emerging
findings.detail: The HRA is overspending on repairs by £1.200m overall, driven by responsive repairs overspend of £2.137m. The council renegotiated the Morgan Sindall contract in November 2025 via a Deed of Variation. Originally estimated to cost £1.757m annually (with £0.807m growth already budgeted), the actual impact is now estimated at £3.000m—a £1.243m underestimate. Additional pressures include higher-than-expected Price per Property (PPP) exclusions (~£0.600m). Additionally, the responsive repairs contract expires 30 September 2027 and the mechanical/engineering contract expires 31 March 2027; both are being reproc­ured simultaneously, introducing demobilisation and performance risks.
findings.matters: Contract renegotiations can carry hidden costs; the 70% underestimate on the DoV suggests weak commercial controls, and simultaneous retendering of two major contracts exposes the HRA to service disruption and cost spikes.
findings.figures: Responsive repairs overspend £2.137m; Deed of Variation originally £1.757m, now £3.000m (underestimate £1.243m); PPP exclusions pressure ~£0.600m
findings.quote: Based on experience during the first six months the DoV has been in operation, the annual impact is now estimated to be approximately £3.000m.

findings.headline: Section 17 (Children in Need) spending overspend masked by £0.750m draw from Crisis Resilience Fund; underlying overspend £0.958m
findings.detail: Children's Services Section 17 is forecast to overspend by £0.208m, but this figure depends on drawing £0.750m from the Crisis and Resilience Fund. Without that draw, the overspend would be £0.958m. This represents spending being funded from a time-limited grant reserve rather than base budget.
findings.matters: Recurring spend funded from one-off reserves is unsustainable; when the Crisis Resilience Fund is exhausted, the council faces a structural deficit in children's in-need services.
findings.figures: Section 17 forecast overspend £0.208m (with reserve); underlying overspend £0.958m (without reserve); Crisis Resilience Fund drawdown £0.750m
findings.quote: This position assumes £0.750m from the Crisis and Resilience Fund. Without this, section 17 would be forecasting an overspend of £0.958m.

findings.headline: School maintained balances fell £3.987m to £1.789m, with deficit balances now £6.590m across 19 schools (43% in deficit)
findings.detail: Maintained schools' total balances dropped sharply year-on-year. Deficit balances increased by £3.409m to £6.590m, with 14 primary schools (48%), 3 secondary schools (43%), 1 special school, and 1 all-through school reporting deficits. Primary schools alone are in deficit by £4.412m.
findings.matters: School deficits are an early signal of financial distress in the education sector; if these schools require council support or if DSG deficits are not resolved, they will transfer to the council's general fund.
findings.figures: Total school balances £1.789m (down £3.987m); deficit balances £6.590m (up £3.409m); 19 schools in deficit; primary deficits £4.412m
findings.quote: A total of 19 Waltham Schools reported a deficit revenue balance at the end of the 2025/26 financial year. Deficit revenue balances represented a total value of £6.590m, an increase of £3.409m since 31st March 2025.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block forecast to overspend by £12.241m, creating cumulative DSG deficit of £26.562m
findings.detail: The High Needs Block is forecast to overspend by £12.241m in 2026/27 alone, taking the total accumulated DSG deficit to £26.562m. The council is eligible for a High Needs Stability Grant of £12.889m but this is contingent on DfE approval of the SEND Reform Plan, which is still awaited in autumn. Without approval, the deficit cannot be offset.
findings.matters: DSG deficits accumulate as unusable reserves; an unapproved SEND plan leaves £13.673m of forward deficit unresolved, effectively a hidden liability that could constrain future borrowing or force revenue budget reallocation.
findings.figures: High Needs Block overspend £12.241m; cumulative DSG deficit £26.562m; High Needs Stability Grant £12.889m (subject to approval)
findings.quote: The overall forecast deficit is £12.241m in year, all in the High Needs Block, taking the total DSG deficit to £26.562m.

findings.headline: Only 84% of 2026/27 savings forecast to be delivered, with £3.385m (18% of target) categorised as high risk
findings.detail: The council set a savings target of £18.678m for 2026/27. At month 3, only £15.750m (84%) is forecast as deliverable. £3.385m is categorised high risk; £2.250m of this (66%) is the TA lease review. Plans are 'currently being developed' for other red savings totalling £1.135m, with £0.881m 'of potential undeliverable/delayed savings'.
findings.matters: Savings slippage at month 3 is a warning signal; if high-risk savings fail, the council faces a further £3.4m budget gap late in the year when mitigation options are limited.
findings.figures: £18.678m savings target; £15.750m forecast (84%); £3.385m high risk; £0.881m potentially undeliverable
findings.quote: At month 3, against the total savings target of £18.678m, £15.750m of savings are forecast to be delivered by the end of the financial year.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation lease conversion saving reproffiled and reduced from £2.250m to £0.130m in-year, with £1.495m pushed to 2027/28
findings.detail: The council planned to convert 161 short-term TA leases to 10+ year terms to increase Housing Benefit subsidy. Originally expected to save £2.250m in-year, a change control has reduced the 2026/27 saving to £0.130m, deferring £1.495m to 2027/28 and £0.484m to 2028/29 (total £2.109m, down from £3.000m). The rationale cites 'lengthy legal processes', 'expected potential rent increase requests', and a reduction in TA households from the snapshot date.
findings.matters: A major planned saving has been substantially reproffiled, indicating underestimation of implementation risk; if the lease programme also faces rent increase requests (3% would cost an additional £0.387m), the saving could evaporate entirely.
findings.figures: Originally £2.250m 2026/27 saving; now £0.130m 2026/27, £1.495m 2027/28, £0.484m 2028/29; potential 3% rent increase risk £0.387m
findings.quote: Rationale: 1. Lengthy legal processes and time to negotiate with landlords, 2. Landlord negotiations: expected potential rent increase requests and associated legal costs, 3. Overall reduction in number of TA households under lease, from when snapshot was taken.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation cost per placement up 4% despite household numbers falling, due to frozen subsidy frozen at 2011 Local Housing Allowance rates
findings.detail: Waltham Forest held 1,535 TA households at end of June 2026, down from 1,705 peak. However, average weekly net cost per placement has risen from £262 (March 2025) to £273 (May 2026). The council receives subsidy frozen at 90% of 2011 LHA rates, so as real accommodation costs rise, the gap widens. The £11.883m HGF overspend is driven almost entirely by TA costs of £11.827m.
findings.matters: TA costs are spinning out of control despite falling headcount; the subsidy-cost gap widening is a structural problem that cannot be solved by reducing numbers alone—it requires either higher subsidy, property acquisition, or demand prevention.
findings.figures: 1,535 households in TA (June 2026, down from 1,705 peak Oct 2025); average weekly cost £273 May 2026 vs £262 March 2025 (4% increase); HGF overspend £11.883m
findings.quote: Despite this reduction, the average weekly net cost per TA placement has increased by over 4%, from £262 in March 2025 to £273 in May 2026, reflecting continued upward pressure on accommodation costs.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care external placements forecast to cost £7.704m more than budgeted, with package complexity and fee inflation outpacing savings efforts
findings.detail: Placement costs are rising faster than anticipated demand. The council budgeted for £1.645m of demand management savings, but gross external placement expenditure is forecast to rise by £7.622m (7%) compared to last year. The document explicitly states this is 'primarily driven by inflation and changes in package costs rather than growth in service user volumes', with Supported Living (£4.163m), Residential Care (£4.055m), and Home Care (£2.044m) as the largest pressures. The forecast notes: 'Should savings not be fully delivered during the financial year, the forecast position will worsen.'
findings.matters: Uncontrolled ASC placement costs are a leading cause of council financial distress; the inability to offset rising unit costs with savings suggests structural budget challenge rather than temporary overspend.
findings.figures: Gross placements overspend £7.622m (7% increase year-on-year); Supported Living £4.163m, Residential Care £4.055m, Home Care £2.044m; demand savings target £1.645m
findings.quote: The forecast overspend on external placements is £7.567m and is the primary driver for the overall Adult Social Care overspend.

findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £19.9m forecast at month 3, with Adult Social Care placements and temporary accommodation driving the pressure
findings.detail: Total Net Revenue Expenditure is forecast to overspend by £19.901m against a budget of £296.533m. Adult Social Care is overspending by £7.521m, primarily driven by external placement costs (£7.704m), while Place directorate's Housing General Fund overspend is £11.883m, almost entirely from temporary accommodation costs.
findings.matters: A month 3 overspend of this scale signals systemic budget pressures that are unlikely to self-correct; it suggests demand-led cost growth is outpacing both budget assumptions and mitigation efforts.
findings.figures: £19.901m overspend on £296.533m budget; Adult Social Care £7.521m overspend; Place £11.883m overspend
findings.quote: Total Net Revenue Expenditure for Service Areas is a forecast overspend of £19.901m at month 3 against a current budget of £296.533m.

findings.paper_title: Housing Strategy Delivery Update - Cabinet report
findings.headline: New building safety and energy efficiency legislation will pressure HRA without corresponding new burdens funding
findings.detail: Section 3.22 states 'the absence of new burdens funding attached to incoming legislation will place additional pressure on the HRA.' Specific requirements include Awaab's Law (damp/mould response), Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard from 2030, and updated Decent Homes Standard from 2035. Currently only 76% of council homes meet EPC C rating.
findings.matters: Unfunded legislative compliance requirements create future financial liabilities that HRA may struggle to meet given existing pressures
findings.figures: Only 76% of homes meet EPC C rating; MEES standard required by 2030; Decent Homes upgrades from 2035
findings.quote: the absence of new burdens funding attached to incoming legislation will place additional pressure on the HRA

findings.paper_title: Housing Strategy Delivery Update - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Capital scheme delivery risk elevated due to borrowing costs and build inflation already impacting pace
findings.detail: Section 7.1.4 identifies 'Delivery risk remains elevated due to borrowing costs, build inflation and scheme viability challenges, which are already impacting pace and deliverability.' This affects multiple capital programmes including TA delivery, acquisitions, regeneration and retrofit schemes.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence capital programmes can be delivered as planned; elevated risk suggests delivery assumptions may not hold
findings.figures: Risk described as 'elevated'; already 'impacting pace and deliverability'
findings.quote: Delivery risk remains elevated due to borrowing costs, build inflation and scheme viability challenges, which are already impacting pace and deliverability.

findings.paper_title: Housing Strategy Delivery Update - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing gave council C2 rating following April 2025 inspection
findings.detail: The Regulator inspected the Housing Service and issued a C2 rating in April 2025. The council is working on an improvement plan with the regulator, but specific compliance issues remain: 13% of homes still non-decent (down from 19%), 61% tenant satisfaction with ASB handling, and only 21% satisfaction with complaints handling.
findings.matters: A C2 regulatory rating indicates governance and compliance weaknesses in a major council service and suggests management control issues
findings.figures: C2 rating; 13% non-decent homes (down from 19%); 61% ASB satisfaction; 21% complaints satisfaction
findings.quote: Following the council's inspection by the Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) and the subsequent C2 rating in April 2025, the Housing Service has met regularly with the RSH to monitor progress of its improvement plan.

findings.paper_title: Housing Strategy Delivery Update - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation spending forecast at £19.9 million despite reductions from peak
findings.detail: The council forecasts spending £19.9m on TA in 2025/26. While household numbers in TA have reduced from 1,710 in September 2025 to 1,527 in April 2026, section 7.1.3 describes this as 'a material General Fund pressure' with 'demand remains structurally high and cost risk persists.'
findings.matters: A material General Fund pressure on TA limits financial flexibility and indicates structural demand the council cannot fully control
findings.figures: £19.9m forecast TA spend for 2025/26; households reduced from 1,710 (September 2025) to 1,527 (April 2026)
findings.quote: we are forecast to spend £19.9m on TA in this financial year alone

findings.headline: Business Rates collection 0.53% behind target due to retail relief changes and business affordability
findings.detail: Business Rates collection at month 3 is 0.53% behind target. This reflects both early-year collection challenges and the impact of reduced retail relief, which has increased business liabilities at a time when businesses report difficulty paying.
findings.matters: Business rates income is more volatile than council tax and dependent on retail sector health. The combination of policy changes (retail relief reduction) and market conditions (business affordability crisis) points to ongoing income pressure that the council cannot directly control.
findings.figures: 0.53% behind target; June 2026 collection at 28.4%
findings.quote: collection is currently 0.53% behind target. This reflects early-year collection challenges, compounded by the reduction in retail relief, which has increased liabilities and impacted businesses' ability to pay.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection 0.33% behind target, driven by affordability impact of CTS scheme changes
findings.detail: Collection at month 3 is running 0.33% behind target. This is attributed to changes to the Council Tax Support (CTS) scheme in the previous year, which reduced support for working-age households and increased their liability. The affordability impact is affecting early-year collection rates.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if income pressures are temporary or structural. Here the council has made a policy choice that reduces support to working-age households in financial difficulty, and is now seeing reduced payment rates as a consequence. This is a structural income pressure, not a collection issue.
findings.figures: 0.33% behind target; June 2026 collection at 27.7%
findings.quote: Council Tax collection is currently 0.33% behind target. This is consistent with the expected impact of last year's Council Tax Support (CTS) scheme changes, which reduced the level of financial support and increased liability for working-age households, affecting affordability and early-year collection.

findings.headline: Council debt at £40.314m with 54% concentrated in Adult Social Care
findings.detail: Total council debt is £40.314m, with £21.645m (54%) owed by adult social care clients. The council is investing £150k in three additional debt recovery officers to reduce the debt position. Largest debt category is 1-4 years overdue and 4+ years overdue, indicating aged, difficult-to-collect debt.
findings.matters: High debt levels, especially in a vulnerable-client service like ASC, signal cash collection problems and potential future write-offs. The investment in recovery officers indicates the council recognises this as a problem but also suggests in-house recovery has been insufficient.
findings.figures: £40.314m total debt; £21.645m in Adult Social Care (54%); £0.150m investment in 3 new debt recovery officers
findings.quote: The Council currently has £40.314m debt outstanding across all directorates, this is a reduction of £0.771m since month 2. The largest level of debt is in Adult Social Care.

findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit of £26.562m with statutory override ending March 2028
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant is running a £12.241m in-year deficit (all in High Needs Block), bringing the total accumulated DSG deficit to £26.562m. The statutory override allowing carry-forward of deficits expires 1 April 2028. The council is awaiting announcement of government support for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits.
findings.matters: A structural funding gap in SEND/High Needs will require resolution by March 2028. If government support does not materialize, the council will need to either find £26.5m+ from reserves or general fund by that date, or face a significant service reduction in special educational provision.
findings.figures: £26.562m total DSG deficit; £12.241m in-year deficit forecast; statutory override ends 1 April 2028
findings.quote: The overall forecast in-year deficit is £12.241m, all in the High Needs Block, taking the total DSG deficit to £26.562m. The government has announced further support for deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 before the statutory override ends from 1 April 2028, however the level of support has not yet been announced.

findings.headline: Savings delivery forecast to fall £2.928m short of the £18.678m target
findings.detail: At month 3, only £9.480m of £18.678m savings have been delivered (51%). The council forecasts 84% delivery by year-end, equivalent to £15.750m. This implies a £2.928m shortfall. Concerning: high-risk savings are only 3% delivered and medium-risk only 7% delivered against their respective targets.
findings.matters: If the 84% forecast proves optimistic, the council will need to find additional funding from reserves or further cuts. The poor delivery of high and medium-risk savings lines suggests the council is struggling with the harder, larger transformational savings.
findings.figures: £15.750m forecast delivery against £18.678m target (84%); High Risk category at 3% delivery rate, Medium Risk at 7%
findings.quote: At month 3, finance forecast delivery of £15.750m delivery against the total target of £18.678m for 2026/27 (84%).

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspending £7.521m with budget rebase underway, indicating structural underbudgeting
findings.detail: ASC is overspending by £7.521m, primarily in external placements due to increasing demand, complexity, and market rate pressures, plus staffing costs. The council has acknowledged the budget is too low and is rebasing it to match demographic need, scheduled for completion by month 6.
findings.matters: Demand-led service is overspending and budget was evidently set too low. ASC is also the source of £21.645m of the council's £40.314m debt. The rebase will increase the baseline budget going forward, creating structural pressure on the medium-term financial strategy.
findings.figures: £7.521m overspend in ASC; £21.645m ASC-related debt out of £40.314m total
findings.quote: Adult Social Care (ASC) is overspending by £7.521m, primarily in external placements driven by increasing demand, complexity and market pressures, together with staffing pressures on in-house services. The budget for ASC is currently being rebased for the level of demand associated with the council's demographic profile.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation costs remain uncontrolled despite reduction in household numbers
findings.detail: TA is the largest single overspend at £11.883m. Critically, the council has reduced the number of households in temporary accommodation in recent months, yet costs have not fallen. This indicates unit cost inflation driven by market conditions rather than volume factors.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether overspends are volume-driven (and could improve if demand reduces) or cost-driven (and will persist regardless of volume). Here the council has demonstrated it can reduce placements but cannot control the cost per placement, suggesting an intractable market problem.
findings.figures: £11.883m overspend; household numbers reduced but costs did not follow
findings.quote: The overspend in the Place Directorate is due to Temporary Accommodation (TA), which is overspending by £11.883m. Whilst the number of households in TA has reduced in recent months, the underlying cost pressures remain and the market and demand remains volatile.

findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £19.901m requiring Exceptional Financial Support at month 3
findings.detail: Council is forecasting a £19.901m overspend on revenue at month 3 (only 25% through the financial year). Strategy to fund this will include drawing on granted Exceptional Financial Support (up to £19m) and corporate balances. The MTFS Refresh will confirm the exact funding plan.
findings.matters: A significant overspend this early in the year indicates structural imbalance. EFS is finite support and cannot be relied on indefinitely; if pressures persist into next year, the council faces a budget gap that will require reserves or further savings.
findings.figures: £19.901m overspend; up to £19m Exceptional Financial Support available
findings.quote: The month 3 forecast for Revenue Expenditure in the General Fund shows a net overspend of £19.901m. The strategy to fund this overspend will be confirmed as part of the MTFS Refresh but will include the use of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) and any available underspends in corporate balances.

findings.headline: Pre-tender cost estimates carry 8% inflation allowance; tender risk could trigger further budget increases
findings.detail: The £18.084m estimate includes 8% inflation allowance (3.93% construction inflation plus 4.07% risk allowance). Cost plans remain pre-tender and will be tested through competitive procurement. Tender returns must be assessed against approved budgets before contract award.
findings.matters: Market construction costs could exceed pre-tender estimates; any increase above £18.084m would require additional borrowing or scheme deferral
findings.figures: 8% total inflation allowance (3.93% construction + 4.07% risk), cost plans pre-tender, two separate procurement packages to be tested
findings.quote: The cost plans include an overall inflation allowance of 8%, comprising 3.93% previously included construction inflation and a further 4.07% risk allowance. The estimates remain pre-tender and will be tested through procurement.

findings.headline: Council committing £17.598m General Fund borrowing to fund housing temporary accommodation (not HRA)
findings.detail: After a £486k Brownfield Land Release Fund grant, net Council funding of £17.598m is expected from General Fund borrowing at assumed 6.32%, with Minimum Revenue Provision modelled over 30 years. Temporary accommodation is a General Fund cost despite being housing-related, putting it outside the Housing Revenue Account.
findings.matters: This major General Fund borrowing commitment increases council debt servicing burden and reduces borrowing headroom; significant constraint if General Fund faces pressure elsewhere
findings.figures: £17.598m net funding requirement, £486k grant received, 6.32% assumed borrowing rate, 30-year MRP annuity
findings.quote: After applying this grant, the net Council funding requirement is £17.598m, expected to be met from General Fund borrowing.

findings.headline: Financial viability depends entirely on unconfirmed £840k annual cost savings from changing service delivery
findings.detail: The business case assumes the new 60 homes will replace higher-cost external temporary accommodation, generating first-year cost avoidance of £840k (£14k per home × 60). The council explicitly states this is not yet an approved or cashable saving and depends on new homes replacing rather than supplementing existing external placements.
findings.matters: If homes supplement external TA rather than replace it, the council services £17.6m borrowing without the anticipated General Fund offset; business case collapses
findings.figures: £840k potential first-year cost avoidance (not approved), £14k per home assumed external TA cost, applied to 60 homes
findings.quote: This is not an approved or cashable saving and depends on the new homes replacing external placements and the associated expenditure reducing.

findings.headline: Capital budget increased by £2.723m (17.7%) above previously approved baseline in nine months
findings.detail: The gross capital budget rose from £15.361m to £18.084m. The council attributes the increase to design development, survey findings, building condition discoveries, market pricing updates, inflation, and revised contingency allowances. Earlier approvals were based on early-stage estimates and limited site information.
findings.matters: Material capital cost escalation on a nine-month timescale indicates estimation weakness or scope creep; further increases are possible as this is pre-tender
findings.figures: £18.084m revised gross budget (was £15.361m), £2.723m increase, 17.7% overrun, previously £0.584m CSAMG approval plus £14.777m Cabinet approval (February 2026)
findings.quote: The revised gross capital budget of £18.084m is therefore £2.723m, or 17.7%, above the approved baseline.

findings.headline: Capital scheme targets £840,000 first-year cost avoidance by replacing externally leased temporary accommodation
findings.detail: The council proposes converting four existing vacant buildings into 60 self-contained temporary accommodation homes. The financial appraisal models potential first-year temporary accommodation cost avoidance of up to £840,000 where new homes replace external placements outside the borough. The scheme involves internal reconfiguration only with no building footprint expansion, and 78% of units are proposed as 2-bedroom or larger family homes.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor councils' capital schemes and their identified financial benefits. An £840,000 annual cost avoidance from repurposing vacant assets would be material to a lending assessment, though the detailed financial appraisal and funding strategy sit in the main Cabinet report.
findings.figures: £840,000 first-year cost avoidance, 60 homes across four sites, 78% proposed to be 2 bedroom or larger
findings.quote: potential first-year temporary accommodation cost avoidance of up to £840,000 where the new homes replace external placements

findings.headline: Borrowing costs and reserve constraints are directly limiting housing development on council land
findings.detail: The council reports delays in identifying viable development sites on its own land, explicitly citing financial pressures including borrowing costs and reserve position alongside market headwinds. Borrowing costs are also named as a barrier for registered provider partners.
findings.matters: Council explicitly identifies that cost of borrowing and reserve position are constraining capital investment, signalling tightening financial flexibility
findings.figures: No borrowing costs or reserve figures disclosed in document
findings.quote: Challenges in identifying viable sites under current council financial pressures - cost to borrow, state of reserves - and market challenges - build costs and inflation

findings.headline: Council cannot find viable financial route for sheltered housing modernization despite acknowledged need
findings.detail: The council has concluded through financial modelling that there is no viable path to deliver a needed modernization of its sheltered housing stock. It acknowledges the stock requires action but notes this will continue to generate financial pressures through maintenance costs on aging facilities.
findings.matters: Deferred capital maintenance on aging council assets due to financial constraint creates future budget pressure and indicates limited financial headroom
findings.figures: No cost forecast provided for deferred maintenance pressure
findings.quote: High level financial modelling has established that there is not currently a viable financial route for the council to take forward the Sheltered scheme review in line with propsals. However, the need to take action, particularly to modernise existing occupied stock will remain and continue to cause financial pressures in maintenance costs.

findings.headline: Building Safety Regulations compliance causing delays to Families & Homes Hub fit-out
findings.detail: The Sunflower House fit-out element of the Families & Homes Hub project has been re-profiled to 2027/28 specifically due to the impact of Building Safety Regulations, indicating compliance work is lengthening project timelines.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance delays on residential projects signal potential for similar issues across the HRA housing delivery programme.
findings.figures: £0.068m underspend; re-profiled to 2027/28.
findings.quote: £0.068m underspend on the Families & Homes Hub project due to re-profiling of forecast spend to 2027/28 in line with the current programme for delivery of the Sunflower House fit-out works, which was delayed due to the impact of Building Safety Regulations.

findings.headline: Soho Theatre Walthamstow project cancelled: £1m fit-out funds no longer required due to commercial leasing plan changes
findings.detail: A £1m commercial fit-out project for the Soho Theatre is being abandoned because the leasing plan for the unit has changed, rendering the investment unnecessary. This represents a capital allocation change and suggests revised commercial strategy.
findings.matters: Cancellation of planned investment signals either weak commercial demand or a strategic pivot that may affect other regeneration plans.
findings.figures: £1.000m underspend; project abandonned entirely.
findings.quote: £1.000m underspend on the Soho Theatre Walthamstow project, relating to the fit out of a commercial unit. Due to changes to the leasing plan of the unit, these funds are no longer required.

findings.headline: Avenue Road regeneration scheme £2m re-profiled pending October Cabinet approval for revised delivery route and budget
findings.detail: A significant HRA housing delivery scheme is held up awaiting Board-level approval of a revised delivery approach. The scheme is £2m underspent in 2026/27 pending this decision, indicating either scope change or budget rebaselining.
findings.matters: Schemes requiring Cabinet approval for revised routes suggest cost or scope uncertainty that could affect project viability or future borrowing.
findings.figures: £2.000m spend re-profiled to 2027/28; approval pending October Cabinet.
findings.quote: £2.000m spend re-profiled to 2027/28 on the Avenue Road regeneration scheme, pending approval of the revised delivery route and budget at October Cabinet.

findings.headline: Multiple major projects delayed by external partners (TfL, NHS, planning) with uncertain timelines
findings.detail: Leyton Underground Station (£8m), Walthamstow Central Station Box (£0.572m), and Leyton Sports Ground are all held up by TfL delivery schedules beyond council control. St James Health Centre fit-out (£3m) delayed by prolonged NHS lease negotiations. Low Hall Depot (£2.4m) awaiting planning approval for August/September start on site.
findings.matters: Schedule dependencies on external parties (TfL, NHS, planning authorities) reduce predictability of capital spend and may extend borrowing periods.
findings.figures: Leyton Underground £8m; Walthamstow Central £0.572m; St James Health Centre £3m; Low Hall Depot £2.4m; re-profiled to 2027/28.
findings.quote: £8.00m underspend on the Leyton Underground Station project – which is fully funded by Strategic Community Infrastructure Levy (SCIL) – due to re-profiling of payments to Transport for London (TfL) to 2027/28 in line with TfL's current delivery programme.

findings.headline: HRA housing stock quality target: reduce non-decency levels from 13% to 8% by March 2027
findings.detail: The council currently has 13% of its HRA housing stock failing to meet the Decent Homes standard as of end 2025/26. It is investing £32.187m in 2026/27 specifically to improve this, with programmes targeting damp, mould, leaks, windows, and kitchens. Success depends on accelerating planned works from a Q1 spend of £3.3m.
findings.matters: Housing quality gaps create hidden revenue pressure through responsive repairs costs and signal asset management challenges that will cost more to fix if deferred.
findings.figures: £32.187m HRA investment; 13% non-decency at end 2025/26; target of 8% by end 2026/27; £25m instructed, £10m pipeline for delivery by end Q2.
findings.quote: Building Fabric and Decent Homes works (damp and mould, leaks, roofs, windows, kitchens, bathroom replacements to reduce non-decency levels from 13% at the end of 2025/26 to 8% at the end of 2026/27) - £11.732m

findings.headline: Capital programme £43.7m underspent with widespread project delays re-profiled to 2027/28 and beyond
findings.detail: The 2026/27 forecast is £43.7m (23%) below the approved budget, with variances across every directorate. Major projects including Priory Court regeneration, schools capital, housing acquisition programmes, and transport schemes are all being re-profiled to future years. This is not a spending problem but a delivery slippage problem.
findings.matters: Persistent re-profiling signals delivery risk and cash-flow timing issues that affect borrowing requirements and debt servicing predictability.
findings.figures: £161.438m forecast vs £205.156m budget (including appropriations); £43.718m variance; re-profiling affects Place (£32.882m underspend), Housing (£9.934m GF, £4.763m HRA).
findings.quote: This is a variance of £27.197m compared to the 2026/27 budget of £188.635m approved by Cabinet in July 2026. This is due to budget corrections following reconciliation of project spend and budget adjustments to reprofile forecast project expenditure into future years

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Housing Strategy delivery Update Summary
findings.headline: Significant investment needed to meet new housing regulations with no new burdens funding identified
findings.detail: The council must meet three new regulatory standards: Awaab's Law (2025), Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard (2030), and Decent Homes Standard (2035). The paper explicitly states there is 'No new burdens funding attached to new legislation' and notes that 13% of council homes remain non-decent. The council is currently investing in energy efficiency (175 upgrades completed, 100 more planned) but the full cost of compliance is not quantified.
findings.matters: Unfunded regulatory compliance represents a future financial commitment with unclear timing and cost; lenders need to know whether the council has budgeted for or found funding sources for these mandatory improvements.
findings.figures: 13% of council homes non-decent; 175 energy-efficiency upgrades completed; 100 more planned
findings.quote: Significant investment needed to meet: Awaab's Law (2025), Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard (2030), Decent Homes Standard (2035). No new burdens funding attached to new legislation

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Housing Strategy delivery Update Summary
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation spending remains a major financial pressure at £19.7m despite improving outcomes
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £19.7m TA spend but showing mixed progress: the number of households in TA fell from 1,710 to 1,527 between September 2025 and April 2026, and out-of-borough placements dropped from 65% to 47%. However, the paper identifies that longer stays and lack of move-on options persist because PRS homes are unaffordable to residents reliant on Local Housing Allowance.
findings.matters: TA is one of the most difficult budget pressures to control and represents a significant drain on council resources; understanding whether improvements will stick matters to lenders assessing financial stability.
findings.figures: £19.7m forecast spend; 1,710 → 1,527 households (Sept 2025–Apr 2026); 65% → 47% out-of-borough placements
findings.quote: TA remains a major financial pressure (£19.7m forecast spend)

findings.headline: £34.3m capital slippage from 2026/27 with acceleration of only £26.5m to 2027/28, netting £7.8m deferred into outer years
findings.detail: Table 3 shows (£34.310m) slippage out of 2026/27 and £26.517m acceleration into 2027/28, a net deferral of £7.8m. This is in addition to the individual project slippages noted above. The pattern—large slippage concentrated in Place directorate and Neighbourhoods—suggests the council has front-loaded its capital programme but is unable to deliver it on schedule.
findings.matters: Persistent capital slippage affects both the council's cash position (if financing is drawn early) and its ability to deliver promised outcomes. For a lender assessing the council's capital strategy credibility and cash management, significant undelivered slippage is a warning sign. For the finance director, it indicates planning assumptions may not be holding.
findings.figures: Slippage (£34.310m), acceleration £26.517m, net deferral £7.793m
findings.quote: Table 3: Slippage/(Acceleration) row shows (34.310) in 2026/27 column, with 26.517 in 2027/28 column

findings.headline: Housing General Fund capital delivery significantly lagging with £9.934m forecast underspend and multiple major project slippages
findings.detail: Table 2 shows Housing (General Fund) budgeted at £55.522m but forecast at only £45.588m — an 18% underspend. Table 7 reveals this is driven by systematic slippage: MHCLG Acquisition Programmes (phases 2-4) deleted or reprofiled (£4.3m-£2.8m each), plus major regeneration projects (EMD Cinema £1.0m, Coronation Square £0.6m, Leyton Sports Ground £0.5m, Families & Homes Hub £0.1m) all reprofiled to 2027/28 or later. The scale and pattern suggest delivery capacity constraints or scheme viability issues.
findings.matters: A council unable to spend 18% of allocated housing capital in-year—particularly on government-backed acquisition programmes—indicates either project pipeline problems or delivery resource constraints. For a lender, this raises questions about the council's capital deployment track record; for the finance director, it suggests either over-optimistic forecasting or real barriers to scheme delivery.
findings.figures: Approved £55.522m, forecast £45.588m, underspend £9.934m; major slippages: Low Hall Depot £2.4m, Housing Acquisitions Phase 2-4 combined £8.3m
findings.quote: Table 7: Multiple entries show 'Budget Reprofiled' for Housing Acquisitions and major projects; Table 2 shows Housing (General Fund) revised budget 2026-27: 55.522, forecast: 45.588, variance: (9.934)

findings.headline: Adult Social Care capital programme forecast to overspend by £2.904m against a £0.132m approved budget
findings.detail: Table 2 shows Adult Social Care with an approved 2026/27 budget of £0.132m but a forecast of £3.036m — a variance of £2.904m (2,200% overspend). This represents a significant unbudgeted capital commitment in adult services, suggesting either unplanned infrastructure needs (possibly in care homes or facilities) or a major forecasting failure in the original budget.
findings.matters: A capital overspend of this magnitude in a traditionally revenue-heavy service indicates either asset condition emergencies, compliance failures, or poor budget planning. For a lender, it signals potential future calls on reserves or borrowing; for the finance director, it flags a control issue.
findings.figures: Approved budget £0.132m, forecast £3.036m, variance £2.904m
findings.quote: Table 2: Adult Social Care – Revised Budget 2026-27: 0.132, 2026-27 Forecast: 3.036, 2026-27 Variance: 2.904

findings.headline: Review of housing delivery company Sixty Bricks underway, with intent to ensure integrated delivery model
findings.detail: The strategy commits to concluding a review of the Council's housing company Sixty Bricks and ensuring an integrated overall housing delivery model. This suggests the current structure may not be delivering effectively or may need restructuring, and introduces uncertainty about future delivery capacity and governance.
findings.matters: Delivery company reviews often precede restructuring, performance issues, or changes to business model; this affects predictability of capital delivery and may signal governance gaps
findings.figures: Sixty Bricks delivered 299 homes since 2018 (220 affordable, 188 social rent)
findings.quote: Conclude the review of the Council's housing company Sixty Bricks and ensure an integrated overall housing delivery model.

findings.headline: High homelessness pressure with 1,757 households owed a duty annually and 8,144 on housing register
findings.detail: During 2021–22, 1,757 households in Waltham Forest were owed a duty under the Homelessness Reduction Act (16.9 per 1,000 residents, above national average of 11.7). This, combined with 8,144 households on the housing register and nearly 1,000 in temporary accommodation, creates ongoing service cost pressures and capital demand for suitable housing.
findings.matters: High homelessness duty and temporary accommodation numbers drive revenue costs and capital needs; if the council cannot reduce these numbers, budgets and HRA cash flow remain under pressure
findings.figures: 1,757 households owed homelessness duty (2021–22); 8,144 on housing register (as of Oct 2023); ~1,000 in temporary accommodation; 16.9 per 1,000 residents owed duty
findings.quote: During the 2021 to 2022 financial year, 1,757 households in Waltham Forest were owed a duty under the Homelessness Reduction Act, equating to 16.9 households per 1,000. This is significantly above the national (11.7 per 1,000) and London (14.7 per 1,100) averages.

findings.headline: Significant capital investment required in existing housing stock quality and energy efficiency
findings.detail: 24% of existing affordable homes are EPC Band D or below, and the council has set a target for 80% of homes to achieve EPC B by 2030. Additionally, 65% of energy efficiency recommendations for properties in the borough would cost homeowners £1,500 or more. This signals substantial retrofit investment will be required, particularly in council-owned stock.
findings.matters: Large-scale retrofit programmes are capital-intensive, can strain budgets if grant funding is insufficient, and may require novel financing arrangements (the council mentions exploring climate bonds and loan schemes)
findings.figures: 24% of affordable homes EPC D or below; 65% of retrofit recommendations cost £1,500+; target 80% EPC B by 2030; 16% of households in fuel poverty
findings.quote: 24% of existing affordable homes in the borough are EPC Band D or below... In 2022, 65% of recommendations to improve the efficiency of properties in the Borough would cost homeowners £1,500 or more.

findings.headline: HRA under pressure from building safety and decent homes compliance, reducing headroom for new investment
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that the cost of upgrading existing council homes to meet decent homes standards and new building safety regulations is creating financial pressure on the Housing Revenue Account. This directly limits the HRA's capacity to invest in new stock. The strategy includes a commitment to review forecasting and borrowing arrangements, suggesting the council is exploring ways to increase HRA borrowing headroom.
findings.matters: HRA headroom constraints directly affect the council's ability to borrow against rental income and increase housing stock, a core part of its financial sustainability and capital delivery
findings.figures: Not specified in this document; 10,000+ council-owned homes requiring compliance work
findings.quote: the cost of upgrading the Council's existing council homes to ensure the decent homes standard is met and new building safety regulations are addressed is placing financial pressures on the Housing Revenue Account (HRA). This serves to reduce the headroom available for investment in new stock.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 - Annual Treasury Management Review -( Full Council) 16th July 2026
findings.headline: Council executed £100m PWLB medium-term borrowing to finance capital expenditure and replace temporary funding
findings.detail: During 2025-26, the council raised £100m in new PWLB medium-term loans, financing capital expenditure and refinancing temporary borrowing. This brought total outstanding debt to £545.5m as at 31 March 2026, with annual interest payable of £20.3m.
findings.matters: A significant borrowing decision that shifts the council's debt from temporary to medium-term PWLB funding. This locks in debt service costs for an extended period and reflects the scale of capital spending the council is funding through long-term borrowing.
findings.figures: £100m PWLB loans, £545.5m total debt outstanding, £20.3m annual interest payable
findings.quote: The Council executed new PWLB medium-term loans of £100m to finance capital expenditure and to replace temporary borrowing.

findings.headline: Section 114 contingency is explicitly identified: if demand pressures prove ongoing or new pressures emerge, balanced-budget achievement may become impossible.
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer states Section 114 is 'unlikely to be needed in the current year' but would be required if pressures are 'established to be on-going or there are new pressures'. This requires MTFS refresh. The council received up to £19m Exceptional Financial Support for 2026/27 based on conservative forecasts, but actual 2025/26 outturn was significantly better (£2.710m actual vs £15.315m forecast reserve use), suggesting EFS assumptions may require reset.
findings.matters: Section 114 notices are formal statutory warnings that a council cannot set a balanced budget and trigger intervention. The CFO's explicit flagging signals low margin for financial error and indicates that adverse demand or grant scenarios could rapidly escalate to statutory intervention.
findings.figures: EFS granted: up to £19m; reserve use forecast at budget time: £15.315m; actual reserve use: £2.710m
findings.quote: Section 114 is unlikely to be needed in the current year. If the pressures are established to be on-going or there are new pressures, they will need to be picked up in the MTFS refresh and potentially could result in a revised budget gap that would need to be resolved using reserves, savings or revised EFS assumptions.

findings.headline: Council Tax and Business Rates collection fell below target, with Business Rates collection described as having 'struggled'.
findings.detail: Council Tax collection achieved 94.79%, missing the 95% target by £402k. Business Rates collection achieved 94.6%, missing the 96% target by £1.033m. The Business Rates shortfall is attributed specifically to businesses struggling to pay following reduction of retail relief from 70% to 40%. Both underscore income volatility and resident/business financial stress.
findings.matters: Collection rates are self-controlled revenue sources. Declining collection signals either customer financial stress, which reduces future income, or collection effectiveness issues, both creating income volatility that must be hedged with reserves or savings.
findings.figures: Council Tax: 94.79% vs 95% target (£402k shortfall); Business Rates: 94.6% vs 96% target (£1.033m shortfall)
findings.quote: The in-year collection rate achieved in relation to Business Rates for 2025/26 is 94.6% (£69.803m), this is 1.4% (£1.033m) below the target of 96%. Collection has struggled this year with the drop in retail relief from 70% to 40% relief, with businesses struggling to meet the charges.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit of £14.320m will consume General Fund resources, with a further £10.340m deficit forecast for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £10.914m in-year, driven by growth in Education, Health and Care Plans and placement costs. Under statutory override the full £14.320m deficit carries forward. The DfE will fund 90% via Stability Grant, but the council must fund the remainder from General Fund. An estimated £10.340m further deficit is forecast for 2027/28, with no yet-announced treatment from DfE.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is a permanent unfunded liability that drains General Fund resources each year to prop up schools' high needs provision. It reduces financial flexibility for other council services and reduces headroom for discretionary spending or borrowing.
findings.figures: In-year High Needs deficit: £10.914m; cumulative DSG deficit: £14.320m; forecasted 2027/28 High Needs deficit: £10.340m
findings.quote: The final position for the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) shows an in-year deficit of £10.914m in the high needs block. This would take the cumulative deficit for high needs to £19.786m at the end of March 2026, with an overall net DSG deficit of £14.320m.

findings.headline: Adults Social Care, Children's Services and Temporary Accommodation overspent by £23.8m, identified as ongoing structural demand pressures.
findings.detail: Adults and Transitions combined overspent by £10.905m; Temporary Accommodation overspent by £12.871m. These service areas are described as experiencing 'significant impact' from demand, 'in line with other Local Authorities' and 'London Boroughs'. The paper describes an overall unfunded directorate budget pressure of £25.231m — money the council spent but has not received funding for.
findings.matters: Demand-led overspends are structural budget gaps, not one-off problems. They signal the council's baseline funding is insufficient for actual service obligations, meaning savings in other areas must continuously offset these pressures or the deficit grows.
findings.figures: Adults and Transitions overspend: £10.905m; Temporary Accommodation overspend: £12.871m; Total unfunded service pressure: £25.231m
findings.quote: The Council, in line with other Local Authorities, is experiencing high demand in relation to both Adults Social Care and Transitions and this has had a significant impact on the service outturn position with a combined overspend of £10.905m. In addition, in line with other London Boroughs there has been a significant overspend in relation to Temporary Accommodation (TA), with an overall overspend of £12.871m.

findings.headline: Budget Strategy Reserve depleted by 73% in a single year, from £13.965m to £3.704m.
findings.detail: Total drawdowns of £10.261m during 2025/26 included £2.216m for transformation programmes, £3.607m for earmarked reserves and provisions, £1.727m in other drawdowns, and £2.710m to fund year-end service overspends. The reserve now provides minimal buffer for unexpected pressures in 2026/27 and beyond.
findings.matters: The Budget Strategy Reserve is the council's primary mechanism for managing in-year demand pressures and funding transformation. Its rapid depletion indicates the council has transitioned from managing financial risk to absorbing it reactively, leaving little capacity for further shocks.
findings.figures: Opening balance £13.965m; closing balance £3.704m; total drawdowns £10.261m
findings.quote: On the 1st of April 2025, the Budget Strategy Reserve (BSR) had a value of £13.965m. After drawdowns totalling £2.216m to fund the Transformation programme; a budgeted earmarked reserves and provisions drawdown of £3.607m; £1.727m in other drawdowns and a drawdown of £2.710m to fund the net service overspend, the balance in the BSR at 31st March 2026 is £3.704m.

findings.headline: Financial sustainability identified as material governance issue requiring ongoing action
findings.detail: The Annual Governance Statement explicitly identifies financial sustainability and audit assurance as material governance issues requiring ongoing action. The Council acknowledges its governance arrangements are under pressure from financial, operational and regulatory challenges. The specific nature of these sustainability concerns is not detailed in this summary.
findings.matters: A council flagging financial sustainability as a material weakness in governance signals potential budget control issues or underlying financial stress that affects creditworthiness
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: There are material governance issues requiring ongoing action, particularly: Financial sustainability and audit assurance

findings.headline: Pension scheme deficit of £208m requiring new triennial valuation at 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The council's Local Government Pension Scheme has assets of £934m against liabilities of £1,142m, creating a material £208m deficit. A new triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025 will be incorporated into the 2026 accounts. The auditors flag risk that small changes in actuarial assumptions (discount rate, inflation, mortality) could significantly affect pension liabilities and the potential asset ceiling.
findings.matters: A material pension deficit affects the council's balance sheet and financial sustainability. If assumptions change materially or the council enters pension surplus, it could shift reserves significantly. A lender needs to understand the pension obligation.
findings.figures: Assets £934m, liabilities £1,142m as at 31 March 2025. Deficit £208m
findings.quote: Fair value of defined benefit plan assets 934 [£m]... Defined benefit plan liabilities (1,142) [£m]

findings.headline: Significant prior audit evidence quality issues that will carry forward into 2025-26 audit
findings.detail: In the 2024-25 audit, the council experienced repeated delays in providing audit responses, provided transaction listings of inadequate quality (including contra-transactions that inflated work scope), and supplied audit evidence that was insufficient or inappropriate. The auditors could not conclude over some balances. These issues are documented as key areas for improvement requiring engagement with management.
findings.matters: Poor audit evidence quality signals weak financial controls and record-keeping. A lender needs assurance that the council maintains reliable financial records and responsive financial management. This also increases audit risk and cost.
findings.figures: Issues unresolved as of July 2026 audit plan publication
findings.quote: Some of the audit evidence provided by management was not sufficient and/or appropriate for the purposes of our testing. Some examples of this was evidence that lacked the clarity needed for the audit team to accept or an internally produced document would be provided which was not sufficient, appropriate audit evidence. Most often, this would result in the audit team rejecting the evidence and would require more time invested by officers and the audit team in gathering and reviewing evidence, reducing efficiency. However, this has also resulted in us being unable to conclude over the various balances.

findings.headline: Council has applied for Exceptional Finance Support from MHCLG to set a balanced 2026-27 budget
findings.detail: The council needed central government bailout funding to balance its budget for the coming year. This follows stated budgetary pressures in previous years. Without this exceptional grant, the council could not set a balanced budget.
findings.matters: A lender considers exceptional support as a red flag. It signals that a council cannot live within its standard funding envelope and needs government intervention. This limits borrowing capacity and raises solvency questions.
findings.figures: EFS applied for to set balanced budget for 2026-27
findings.quote: The Council has faced budgetary pressures in previous years and has applied for Exceptional Finance Support (EFS) from the Ministry of Housing, Communities, & Local Government (MHCLG) to set a balanced budget for 26/27.

findings.headline: Council forecasting £32.97m services overspend mitigated by £17.66m underspends, leaving a net pressure of £15.32m in 2025-26
findings.detail: As at month 9 of 2025-26, the council's operational services are forecasting a significant overspend. While this is partially offset by corporate underspends and additional income, the net budget pressure of £15.32m represents material variance from the approved budget. The auditors' assessment is that the council is forecasting an immaterial deficit position.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council can control spending within budget. A £15.32m net overspend (or £32.97m before mitigation) in a single year signals either spending control issues or that the budget was set incorrectly. This is live variance, not forecast.
findings.figures: Services overspend £32.97m, mitigated by £17.66m underspends, net pressure £15.32m
findings.quote: the Council has faced difficulties in delivering the 25/26 budget, with a forecasted services overspend of £32.97m as at month 9. This is mitigated by underspends and/or additional income of £17.66m in corporate budgets and therefore the net pressure is £15.32m.

findings.headline: Four consecutive years of unaudited accounts ended but assurance is still being rebuilt
findings.detail: The council received disclaimed opinions for 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25. The auditors are now undertaking a separate rebuilding assurance process to re-establish confidence in previously unaudited periods. The auditors are still completing their rebuilding assurance risk assessment and will report separately once finished.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's accounts were verifiable. Four years of disclaimed opinions means nobody could verify the financial position. Even if the 2025-26 audit opinion is issued, the prior period history is material credit risk.
findings.figures: Disclaimers issued for 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25
findings.quote: For London Borough of Waltham Forest, this had the impact of two disclaimers of opinion, issued by your predecessor auditor, for the two financial years up to and including 2022/23. We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 28 February 2025 to comply with the statutory backstop date as reported to your previously. For the 2024/25 external audit, we issued a disclaimer of opinion on 25 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council will receive £22m capital receipt in January 2027 to fund transformation costs and staff severance
findings.detail: The council is using Flexible Use of Capital Receipts to fund the 'cost of change' - transformation investment, redundancy and pension strain costs. This capital receipt is central to enabling the £40m+ savings through investment in change management and workforce restructuring. Close monitoring of return on investment is required.
findings.matters: This affects the council's cash flow timing and capital position. The January 2027 receipt date is material for understanding when funds become available for transformation spending. The model depends on delivering promised savings to justify the transformation investment.
findings.figures: £22 million capital receipt, January 2027
findings.quote: The Council will receive a capital receipt of £22 million in January 2027 and this will be utilised to fund both transformation costs and severance costs (i.e. both redundancy and pension strain) over the next two years.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support is explicitly time-limited, with financial sustainability target of 2029/30
findings.detail: The council has until 2029/30 (three years from this report) to achieve a balanced budget position without further government support. The paper describes this as 'a critical but time limited opportunity'. After that date, the council must be financially independent.
findings.matters: Time-limited support creates urgency and defines the deadline for transformation success. If the council fails to achieve sustainability by 2029/30, there is no indication of further government support available, creating risk for any lending decisions.
findings.figures: Deadline: 2029/30
findings.quote: Exceptional Financial Support offers a critical but time limited opportunity to stabilise the Council's financial position so that a balanced budget position can be achieved without the need for further support in the future.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: CIPFA Resilience Review found the council's previous 'salami-slicing' approach was insufficient and genuine transformation is needed
findings.detail: The November 2025 CIPFA review, commissioned as part of EFS preparation, identified that the council had relied on tactical and incremental cuts rather than systemic redesign. This suggests past financial management approaches did not work, explaining why EFS became necessary.
findings.matters: If a council has already tried cost-cutting without achieving sustainability, this indicates either past mismanagement or structural problems. The finding that deeper transformation is needed suggests the previous approach was inadequate and the challenges are more fundamental.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The review highlighted the need to move away from approaches that rely on 'salami-slicing' and tactical headcount reduction, rather than genuine, cross-cutting redesign.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council has already delivered over £140m in savings over the past decade
findings.detail: This history of substantial cost reductions means the council has exhausted many of the easier savings options. The paper notes that previous attempts used 'salami-slicing' and tactical cuts which proved insufficient, requiring deeper transformation now.
findings.matters: Previous savings of this scale indicate the council has limited fat remaining to trim. Future savings will be harder to find and more likely to impact service delivery or capacity.
findings.figures: over £140m savings delivered
findings.quote: After more than a decade of reduced funding from government and the delivery of over £140m savings, we need to radically rethink our offer if we are to achieve financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Seventy-two pence of every pound spent supports vulnerable services, with demand rising faster than resources
findings.detail: The council identifies this as one of three core realities driving financial pressure. Vulnerable services (social care, children's services, support for vulnerable adults) are demand-led and rising. This spending is largely uncontrollable by the council and creates structural budget pressure independent of council decisions.
findings.matters: Demand-led services are difficult to cut without policy change or service rationing. Rising demand on a fixed or declining budget means the structural deficit is likely to persist unless underlying demand patterns change or additional funding is provided.
findings.figures: 72p in every £1
findings.quote: 72p in every £1 the Council spends supports the most vulnerable, caused by demand continuing to rise faster than resources.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Council must deliver £42.1m in savings over three years to achieve financial sustainability by 2029/30
findings.detail: The Mission Waltham Forest Transformation Programme targets £42.1m in savings over the next three years, with £40m+ coming from transformation activity. The council achieved £16.81m in the current year (2025/26) and is on track, but this sets the required pace for future years. The savings are based on a cost-of-change investment model.
findings.matters: This represents the scale of organisational change required. Lenders need to assess whether this savings plan is credible and achievable without undermining service delivery or financial position further.
findings.figures: £42.1m over three years; £40m from transformation; £16.81m achieved in 2025/26
findings.quote: Over the next three years, we will use this methodology to deliver £42.1m savings.

findings.paper_title: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) Mobilisation - Cabinet report
findings.headline: Waltham Forest has been granted Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG, placing it under government financial oversight
findings.detail: The council has received formal agreement for EFS from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. This is government support for councils in financial difficulty, indicating the council reached a point where it could not balance its budget without intervention. The support comes with specific requirements for transformation, governance, and delivery of savings.
findings.matters: EFS is a marker of serious financial stress and brings enhanced government scrutiny. Lenders need to understand that this council is under government intervention and has specific obligations to return to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: EFS level incorporated in 2026/27 Budget Report
findings.quote: MHCLG have agreed in principle the level of EFS as incorporated within the 2026/27 Budget Report.

findings.headline: Capital projects require additional Greater London Authority grant funding to address viability challenges and enable continued delivery
findings.detail: The council reports taking 'robust leadership' with construction and development partners to maintain project delivery despite challenging market conditions. This includes securing 'in principle agreement' to significant GLA grant funding and exploring alternative funding models specifically to address 'viability challenges'. This suggests projects are not financially viable at current costs without additional external funding.
findings.matters: Projects requiring external grant support to achieve viability indicates cost pressures on the delivery programme and dependence on ongoing government funding to meet capital objectives.
findings.figures: Significant level of GLA grant (unquantified in this paper)
findings.quote: This includes securing in principle agreement to a significant level of Greater London Authority (GLA) grant and exploring other funding models to address viability challenges and support continued delivery of the programme.

findings.headline: Capital Prioritisation Framework introduced in 2024 in response to high inflation, rising construction costs, and increased capital borrowing costs placing pressure on the Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.detail: In February 2024, Cabinet endorsed a new framework that restricts capital spending to schemes in construction, contractually obliged schemes, statutory compliance, schemes protecting the MTFS, and externally-funded projects. This framework was implemented specifically because inflation, construction cost rises, and increased borrowing costs had created unsustainable pressure on the council's medium-term finances.
findings.matters: The need to implement a restrictive capital prioritisation framework demonstrates that the council has had to constrain discretionary capital spending due to cost pressures, indicating financial strain.
findings.figures: Framework implemented February 2024
findings.quote: In February 2024, Cabinet endorsed the implementation of a new Capital Prioritisation Framework to support prudent financial management. The Framework was implemented in response to the risks of high inflation and rising construction costs, alongside increased capital borrowing costs, which have placed additional pressure on the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS).

findings.headline: Capital programme will cost £64.6 million in General Fund revenue over ten years, with £58.85 million of interest costs on borrowing
findings.detail: The finance section details the revenue implications of the capital programme, which are built into the MTFS. Interest costs alone are projected at £58.85 million over the decade to 2035/36, with an additional £5.75 million for Minimum Revenue Provision. This represents an ongoing revenue commitment arising from the capital programme's borrowing needs.
findings.matters: The substantial interest burden shows how much of future revenue budgets will be consumed by debt servicing, constraining flexibility for service delivery and other priorities.
findings.figures: £64.6 million total GF revenue cost; £58.85 million interest payable; £5.75 million MRP
findings.quote: Over the term of the Capital Investment Strategy (from 2025/26 to 2035/36), the GF revenue cost of the Capital Programme is estimated at £64.6 million, made up of projected interest payable of £58.85 million and MRP of £5.75 million.

findings.headline: Council applying for Exceptional Financial Support totalling up to £63 million across three years to manage revenue budget pressures
findings.detail: The council has applied for EFS of £19 million for 2026/27, an estimated £19 million for 2027/28, and £25 million for 2028/29. This support does not form part of the capital programme but impacts the council's borrowing needs and debt repayment obligations. The amounts indicate underlying revenue pressures beyond the council's normal budget capacity.
findings.matters: EFS applications signal that the council cannot balance its revenue budget within normal resources and requires government support, which indicates financial stress relevant to any lender assessing creditworthiness.
findings.quote: The council has made an application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £19 million for 2026/27, an estimated £19 million for 2027/28 and £25 million for 2028/29 to manage the estimated pressures on revenue budgets.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme delivered £17.6m below spend in 2024/25 with acknowledged risks of recurrence
findings.detail: The TMSS records 'the HRA capital spend slipped by £17.6m' in 2024/25 and, while recovery is forecast for 2025/26 onwards, explicitly notes 'there remains the risk of further slippage in future years.' Capital delivery problems can push borrowing into periods of higher interest rates.
findings.matters: Repeated capital slippage signals project management weakness and delays debt repayment timelines, extending the period over which financing costs will be incurred.
findings.figures: £17.6m HRA capital slippage in 2024/25
findings.quote: the HRA capital spend slipped by £17.6m. The slippage in expenditure is forecast to be recovered in 2025/26 and subsequent years. However, there remains the risk of further slippage in future years.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increases over the medium term, driving up financing costs as a share of revenue budget
findings.detail: The CFR will increase over the forecast period, with the executive summary noting financing costs will 'rise modestly before stabilising'. The document explicitly states 'the capital financing charge to revenue, the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) will increase, reflecting the capital spending plans.'
findings.matters: Rising financing costs reduce revenue available for service delivery. Increasing debt burden must be serviced from operating budgets and constrains financial flexibility.
findings.figures: CFR forecast in Table 3; financing cost ratios in Table 5 show increases before stabilisation
findings.quote: the capital financing charge to revenue, the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) will increase, reflecting the capital spending plans.

findings.headline: Core cash balances have fallen significantly below the council's £50m liquidity target, with increasing reliance on temporary borrowing
findings.detail: Core cash and short-term investments totalled only £26m as at 31 December 2025, against a £50m liquidity buffer target. The document states 'as the Council's reserves are reducing, temporary borrowing and short-term fixed PWLB loans borrowing facilities are utilised', with temporary borrowing standing at £68.4m. This indicates financial pressure and growing dependence on short-term funding.
findings.matters: Declining reserves and rising temporary borrowing indicate cash pressure and refinancing risk. If reserves continue to deteriorate, the council may face liquidity stress and higher borrowing costs.
findings.figures: Core cash £26m actual vs £50m target; temporary borrowing £68.4m
findings.quote: as the Council's reserves are reducing, temporary borrowing and short-term fixed PWLB loans borrowing facilities are utilised. On 31st December 2025 temporary borrowing stands £68.4m.

findings.headline: The 2026/27 budget is contingent on central government approving £19 million of Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The Treasury Management Strategy states the balanced budget 'includes an application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £19 million from central government and is contingent on that being agreed.' The application seeks permission to fund this support from borrowing. If government does not approve, the budget will not balance.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can balance its budget without contingency on government approval. If EFS is refused, the council will face a budget gap.
findings.figures: £19 million EFS required for 2026/27 budget to balance
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget for the Council sets out a balanced budget position. However, this includes an application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £19 million from central government and is contingent on that being agreed.

findings.headline: Supplier failures have begun occurring in the past year due to financial challenges and employer cost pressures
findings.detail: Several council suppliers have ceased trading during the past year, forcing the council to find mitigation and in some cases incur additional delivery costs at short notice. This is flagged as a new risk.
findings.matters: Supplier failure is a leading indicator of financial distress in the supply base. It signals that cost pressures are acute enough to be forcing exits, and suggests more may follow.
findings.figures: "A few" suppliers; no specific number given
findings.quote: During the past year, a few of the Council's suppliers have ceased trading due to their own financial challenges which also include the additional Employer costs.

findings.headline: North London Waste Authority plant replacement will create a cost cliff-edge within the next few years
findings.detail: The NLWA is replacing the facility that services the council. This will add significant financial pressure, potentially requiring service reductions to balance the budget. The council is using an NLWA smoothing reserve and has implemented food waste separation and recycling initiatives to manage levy share.
findings.matters: This is a committed future cost (plant replacement is happening) with no discretion. The timing and quantum are uncertain but material enough to flag as a strategic risk. The council has already achieved the lowest NLWA levy share in the authority area.
findings.figures: No quantum given; timing described as 'next few years'
findings.quote: The plant that services North London is being replaced which would add a significant financial pressure on the Council in the next few years. A cliff-edge in increased costs following the replacement plant would place significant pressure on the Council's budget and result in service reductions being needed to balance the budget

findings.headline: Delivery risk on agreed savings programme, with non-delivery potentially requiring use of reserves or further Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The council acknowledges risk that agreed MTFS savings may not be achieved or slip into future years, and that the transformation programme may not deliver required savings. The 2026/27 budget includes a £12m contingency, partly to cover savings slippage.
